Understandability and Coherence.explanation: I think the story holds together well. It is a series of vignettes, but seems to be tied together by the central relationship between the narrator and Carl.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: I don't think the story makes sophisticated use of these devices. The strength of the language is the way it blends violence and sex, and contrasts filth and cleanliness throughout the story. It is a sophisticated use of language, but I don't think it fall into the categories of idiom, metaphor, or literary allusion.

Narrative Ending.explanation: I suspect I don't understand the reference at the end to Jansson's temptation. The end didn't make much sense, but I suspect there is meaning there that I am missing!

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The pacing seems balanced. The language is somewhat halting, but the narrative is driven along at a good pace. Nothing drags, or feels skipped over.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: I think there is good balance here. A good example is this paragraph: "I give Carl severe shortness of breath. He misses his exam. Hisses into the hospital phone that I’m killing him. I’m crying. I like Carl. He didn’t beat me up. He gave me a slap. As you do in his circles. You hunt, shoot birds, decontaminate, dole out slaps. You don’t lie. You withhold love. I say I’m sorry. Sorry for being cowardly and unclear. For not knowing much about integrity and honor. But I don’t understand what’s being said. The mix of words and actions, tenderness, violence." It is a conversation on the phone with Carl in the hospital, but mediated through the narrator's thoughts and interpretation. We get both scene and exposition together.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The fight with Carl at the costume party, and the narrator's leaving with the other Practical Pig is the surprising, interesting turn. It is the climax of the tension between Carl and the narrator, and ends in an unexpected way. Yet, it is not unbelievable, and fits the contours of the story as a whole.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: I think we get a good sense of Carl, Martin, Lizzy, and Johan, through the narrator's description of them, although the point of view is always that of the narrator.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: I think the story is successful in balancing the action and the interior thoughts of the narrator. For example, this paragraph: "When Martin drags himself to lectures, I borrow his porn mags, which he keeps in a rattan magazine stand that may once have held yarn or knitting patterns. A small boatneck sailor shirt for a grandchild. A beanie with a pompom on it. I think Martin harbors a lot of tenderness." We have all at once the action (borrowing the porn mags, description of the magazine stand), along with the narrator's imagination (what the stand might have held, and what it means for Martin's personality).

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: I don't think the form and structure are particularly original.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I think the reader comes away thinking about the seeming contradictions in human relationships. The narrator apologizes to Carl for being cowardly and unclear at the end. Yet, I think the reader has the sense that Carl is the one who has been cowardly and unclear. The narrator feels comfortable and close to him, but is never really clear about what he feels for her. The contradictions are highlighted by language that emphasizes contrasts in filth and cleanliness, sex and violence.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story feels original, and avoids cliches.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The story is very successful at evoking a believable material world with a minimum of text. An example is the description of Martin: his ring, the baby food click, wrapped in a blanket, grunting. Other examples include the description of the centerfold, and Johan's description of the smell between teeth.

Character Development.explanation: At first, I thought this story passed this test, on second thought I actually think each character could be developed more. Each seems to be fulfilling a particular character type, rather than being a fully-formed, complex person.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: I think the themes of cleanliness and filth, disgust and love, sex and violence, go a long way in highlighting the complexity at the center of the story, which is the narrator's conflicted relationship with Carl.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story feels a bit unbalanced and unsatisfying. A lot of space is spent on explaining how Jane looks after her friends too much, and then the end of the story is very abrupt and not very interesting. In the beginning we are told Lizzy was agonizing over Martin's unanswered text, but then we learn Martin was pining for Lizzy, who was ignoring him. This was confusing.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The metaphors seem like cliches and aren't very effective. Example: "Jane grasped Johan's hand tightly, navigating into uncharted waters with her compass pointing due north, toward the future - and toward love.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending feels abrupt and unsatisfying. We aren't really invested in Jane's relationship with Johan, and their conversation feels very unnatural. It is like a bullet-point summary of a real conversation.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The story starts to feel repetitive and drags in the middle. There is too much exposition on Jane's problem, i.e. helping those around her who take her for granted.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: Again, the problem here is too much exposition in the middle part of the story. When we get to the final scene, it feels too stilted and abrupt, not like a natural conversation.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There is not much surprising. The climactic ending is a let down, because there is little emotional build-up or complexity.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The perspectives of the characters (other than Jane) are not developed.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation:
There is too much of Jane's interior world here. The conversation between people is too brief to give the reader a sense of the "exterior" world. For example: How's the garage band going?" 
"It's tough, but we're making it work. How about you?" 
"The usual," she said, with a wry smile. More description of the scene, or more conversation would be helpful here.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: There is nothing original about the form or structure.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: There is nothing much for the reader to take away from this story. The reader understands that Jane makes herself too emotionally available to her friends, then decides not to, and gets together with Johan. It is a very flat, uninteresting story.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story does use cliches, such as "To face the seas of uncertainty, confront her fear of vulnerability, and finally start her own odyssey into the unknown?" or "Her friends saw her as the dependable one, the shoulder to cry on, the rational center of their universe. Inside, though, her own world was as chaotic as theirs. While everyone else stumbled toward love, she remained stuck in place, helping guide their journeys but unable to embark on her own.

World Building and Setting.explanation: I thought there wasn't enough description of the physical world, and the action outside of Jane's inner thoughts. Where there is detail sometimes the passages are awkward; for example, "The morning sun streamed through her curtains as Jane headed to her favorite coffee shop, needing a dose of comfort and familiarity." If she is heading to the coffee shop, her attention (and thus the reader's) would not be on the curtains in her home.

Character Development.explanation: The characters are flat and not developed. There needs to be more physical description, backstory, and conversational dialog.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There doesn't seem to be much rhetorical complexity. The meaning of the story seems to be on the surface, and there are few themes or ideas developed beyond the description of the action and the narrator's explicit thoughts about them.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The main problem with this story is that it seems like the preliminary sketch or outline for a fully developed story. The plot points are all there, but there is little detail to help the reader understand why people think what they do, make the decisions they do, or to make the story interesting.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The language is vague throughout. The story does not make sophisticated use of these devices.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The end of the story feels unsatisfying because even though we are told all of the conflict has been resolved, we don't really know anything about the details that brought the main character to that point. The source of the conflict was not apparent and wasn't felt by the reader. We don't even know what her famous research was about!

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The story passes over important incidents too quickly, in a way that does not allow the reader to really understand what happened. For example: "Gradually, they started exchanging notes and discussing class assignments. Carl became her study partner, and soon, a romance began to blossom." What was it about Carl that Emma liked? Another example: "They explored hidden gems, swam in crystal-clear lakes, and danced under starlit skies. Emma found herself laughing more, feeling alive and free. She knew that she had made the right decision." More detail is needed here to understand what they did on the road trip, and why it was such a turning point for Emma.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: Scenes are not described with enough detail. It reads like an outline where details will be filled in later.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The return of Carl to the story was a good twist, and it seemed appropriate to the story. However, like much of the rest of the story, we don't really know why this gave a sense of closure and peace to Emma.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: We don't get the perspectives of characters besides Emma, and even this is unsatisfactorily simple and undeveloped.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Too much of the story is driven along by vague summary of what happened. We don't get much of either the interior world of Emma, or of the action outside.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: Not original in form or structure

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: There is nothing original or interesting about this story because it is so vague. It feels like reading a long synopsis on the book jacket.

Originality in Thought.explanation: There are plenty of cliches, for example, "embark on a journey of self-discovery"; "It was a crossroads"; "her journey of introspection and personal growth.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The story requires more detail to create a vivid and believable world.

Character Development.explanation: None of the characters are developed through dialog, description, or historical back story.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There seems to be little going on below the surface here, and even the surface is vague and uninteresting.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: I would have said this story passed this test, except for the ending did not seem to work with the rest of the story. It felt abrupt and disconnected to the rest of the story.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: This story does pretty well with metaphor. For example, I thought these were effective: "like heavy coins in a rusted tin box"; "It was as if he was now a silhouette, ever-present but never in focus"; "like hot wax dripping onto Stella's hand and filling in the spaces between her fingers." Others were not effective, such as this mixed metaphor: "She knew there would always be room for him on her mental canvas, and that the intricate threads weaving her past to her present and future would continue to bear his shadow.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending felt abrupt and disconnected from the rest of the story. Carl is introduced for the first time here, and it feels like more space is needed to develop his character.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The pacing seemed right for the most part, it did not feel too stretched or compressed.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: There are places where more description and detail from the scene is needed. For example, in this passage: ""Hey, Stella! he cried earnestly, though he made no effort to push past the gaggle of hungry seniors. The hunger insinuated itself into Stella's memories, a concept that seemed symptomatic to her past but which she could not comprehend. The hunger she had felt earlier was somewhat satiated, but she knew it would never be entirely extinguished. These were the markers of Martin’s initial lodgment on her equilibrium scale: an earnest expression devoid of any shyness or uncertainty, and an ability to tug at her sense of self-worth with every follicle of awareness he was able to draw from her. In those moments, she had no idea that they would keep locked together in this delicate dance, cosmic entities tethered by a gravitational, inexplicable bond." What was the delicate dance that locked them together? All we know is that he said "Hey, Stella" to her.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: The shifting of the narrative to different characters kept the story interesting. However, these vignettes centered around each character are not as cohesive as those in Story 1, where the connections of the supporting characters to each other, as well as to the main character, were better explained.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: I think we only really get the perspective of Stella in this story.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: I think the balance is too much on the side of Stella's interior world, and more detail and dialog could be devoted to the action happening around her. The scenes at the departmental reception and the campus shop feel like they need more description of the surrounding action.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: I don't think form or structure is original

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I don't think there is much here for the reader to take away, although it is more interesting than Stories 2 and 3. This story needs more attention to ways to connect the supporting characters to each other. Each is connected to Stella in some interesting way, but their relationships to each other (and thus their significance to Stella) are not developed as much as they could be.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The language seems original, if strange at times. For example, in this paragraph: "Hey, Stella! he cried earnestly, though he made no effort to push past the gaggle of hungry seniors. The hunger insinuated itself into Stella's memories, a concept that seemed symptomatic to her past but which she could not comprehend. The hunger she had felt earlier was somewhat satiated, but she knew it would never be entirely extinguished." The "hunger" seems literal at the beginning of the paragraph, but figurative by the end.

World Building and Setting.explanation: More detail about the physical world, the things and actions surrounding Stella, would improve the story.

Character Development.explanation: Most of the characters are not developed very well, and seem to be character types rather than real people, much in the same way as in Story 1.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: This story does pretty well with metaphor and figurative language, as well as with interesting, fairly complex description of characters and the main character's thoughts. However, I don't think there is a great deal of meaning developed, through symbolism, or the elaboration of literary themes, beyond the surface meaning.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: Yes and no -- the technical answer to the question is that, yes, the pieces of the story work together to form a whole. The story details the narrator's romantic and relationships with several men in her life, and advances somewhat chronologically. (They're sleeping with Carl, then starts to date Johan, then Carl finds out and is upset, and then things don't work out with Johan.) However, there's no plot to be found here -- the story just chronicles the various relationships and then ends.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: I don't know about sophisticated, but there are allusions present in the text. Some work -- "Her lower back arches under the weight of her own willingness, and the cartridge belt burns into her skin like the lick of a whip. Or does it offer relief, like a doctor’s cool fingertips searching for an inflamed tendon?" And some don't -- "He looks like a member of the Ku Klux Klan. The American South. Mangrove swamps. Banjo on the porch. Root beer. Cornbread. Vio- lence. The heart is a lonely hunter." But they're there!

Narrative Ending.explanation: Technically there's no way that this story could end that would feel natural and earned, since there's no plot and therefore no it can't end in a particularly satisfying way. But both Johan and Carl end their relationships with the narrator, and then the story just... stops. Technically, this is a natural ending to the story, since the story was about these two relationships. But the fact that the story doesn't extend beyond the relationships at all makes me wonder why we read it in the first place. Does the narrator not have any worth outside of these two men? Is the only reason their story is interesting because it intersects with Johan and Carl? It makes me wonder what the point was.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The story seems to progress chronologically -- there are no scenes, things are just described, but the two relationships both progress from a beginning to an end.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: There are no real scenes to be found. I suppose you could argue that certain moments like the costume party are scenes, but I personally wouldn't really consider two paragraphs of description a scene. Most key events are summary: "Johan says that he isn’t in love with me. He likes me. He’s interested in me. But I don’t have it in me anymore. I can’t be wearing Johan’s clothes. They don’t fit me. I can barely move. Nothing is disgusting.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: Yes and no -- there are some interesting, and unexpected, moments, such as the teeth moment with Johan. ("Johan says this: "The smell between the teeth, the one that comes out when you floss, is disgusting. Absolutely disgusting."") But I wouldn't say that's a turn, or particularly surprising. Ultimately, we don't know enough about the narrator, Carl, Johan, or their relationships to feel surprised about anything that takes place.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The characters are all given their moment to shine -- such as Johan's "teeth" moment above, finding the condoms under Johan's bed, etc. Again, there's not really enough about these characters to feel inaccurate; you could tell me anything about them and I'd believe it because they're still blank sketches at this point. I wouldn't say that any of the characters are unlikable; they all seem to have pretty surface-level relationships with one another.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: As mentioned earlier, there are attempts at interiority and exteriority, but they mostly fall flat. Take, for example, the final paragraph. ("I think of temptation itself. What it is. Of being able to give a correct description of the Venus of Willendorf. Of being on all fours with a machine gun. Of arching. Being wide open. And listening for the click.") It's clearly an attempt to be profound and sit inside the narrator's head, but if you really read it, it's just meaningless.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The writing isn't bad, but there's nothing original about it. It's just a story about a person in two shitty relationships that end.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: Per the above: it's really just a story about a person in two shitty relationships that end. There are no takeaways, there are no profound insights, we don't even get a sense of character growth.

Originality in Thought.explanation: There are no clichéd phrases that I can remember, but the entire premise of this story is a huge cliché. I mean, come on? Again: a story that aims at literary pretension about two surface-level and failed sexual relationships? That's about as cliché as they come. ("Cat Person," for one.)

World Building and Setting.explanation: Yes and no. I wouldn't say there are really scenes here -- and, thus, the opportunities for sensory details are few and far between -- but one of the most evocative sections is about the black mold in the beginning, which feels sensory, so I'll give it to them.

Character Development.explanation: Zero character development! The character doesn't learn anything or change in any way. I mean, refer to the last paragraph that I pasted in an earlier answer. What does that even mean?!

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: Very surface level. As discussed in earlier answers, there's no complexity, no takeaways, and no growth. It just describes a situation that once was and now is not, and none of the parties seem particularly changed by it.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: Yes -- we get a sense of all of the different players in Jane's life (Lizzy, Carl, Johan, Martin) and how they drain and buoy her in turn. Each character adds up to influence her climactic decision to focus on herself and commit to her relationship with Johan.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: Not really -- it's a simple story, and I don't think that it really needed metaphor or allusion to succeed. I didn't miss it. But of course that doesn't change the answer to this question: that it wasn't present. Well... I guess kind of? "Jane finally cast off her anchor, embarking on a journey propelled by the most powerful force of all. Jane grasped Johan's hand tightly, navigating into uncharted waters with her compass pointing due north, toward the future - and toward love." At the end that's an allusion, I guess.

Narrative Ending.explanation: As per my earlier answer, it's clear how all of the different characters and their weight on Jane's life led her to setting boundaries and focusing on herself, entering into her new relationship with Johan.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The story takes place over a couple of scenes set over two subsequent days. Each scene feels like it's given equal consideration and weight.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: There are multiple scenes -- Jane wanting to text Carl, Jane consoling Martin, Jane at the coffee shop, Jane meeting Johan -- and summaries, like Jane lying in bed at night considering her life.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: I wouldn't say there are any turns in the story -- everything felt pretty in-tune, forecast, and expected.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The story fleetingly touches on other characters like Lizzy and Martin. They're not given any narrative weight at all, but we do understand who they are and why they do what they do.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: Yes, the story does this well. We get a good sense of Jane's interiority. ("Jane gazed out her window at the inky sky, taking a deep breath. Did she have the courage to cut herself loose? To face the seas of uncertainty, confront her fear of vulnerability, and finally start her own odyssey into the unknown?") But there's also a good amount of exteriority, as well. (""I'm saying I'm done running. That I want you, and only you. If you'll have me." Jane smiled, warmth flooding through her as she pulled him into a kiss.")

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: To be clear, I don't think this story needs originality in form or structure. But, no, it's told chronologically, it's very straightforward, and things progress in a linear fashion.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: Technically? It doesn't really seem like an outright "message" of the book, but Jane does quite a bit of ruminating on the need to set boundaries with friends who take or expect too much from her, and it's only once those boundaries are set that she's able to take the next step in deepening her relationship with Johan. It's very possible that the reader might take that message -- the importance of boundaries and protecting your inner peace -- into their own life.

Originality in Thought.explanation: Again, I don't think that this is a bad thing. But the whole "angsty college student figuring out how to manage friendships and a situationship" scenario isn't exactly original.

World Building and Setting.explanation: There are good sensory details throughout. ("The familiar music of The Smiths drifted through the paper-thin dorm walls again as Lizzy agonized over Martin's unanswered text.")

Character Development.explanation: As discussed earlier, Jane goes on a clear emotional journey throughout the story. At the beginning, she feels that she's being emotionally overloaded by the drama and struggles of her friends. In the middle, she decides that she needs to set boundaries and focus on herself. At the end, she has the bandwidth to pursue a relationship with Johan.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: Although there all multiple levels of meaning here -- there's the inciting action, Jane's reaction to it, etc. -- they're all surface-level. Everything, from Jane's realization about boundaries to her decision to pursue Johan, is very explicitly stated.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: Yes, everything in the story was linked and related, from Emma's relationship with her friends Lizzy and Martin to her relationship with her boyfriend Carl and how letting go of Carl and investing more time in her own creative pursuits allowed her to thrive in college and her academic research.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: There aren't really any idioms, metaphors, or allusions present in the story.

Narrative Ending.explanation: Yes and no -- the end of the story did feel natural and earned, as it "flashed forward" and showed Emma's successes, which were made possible by her journey of growth and the fact that she recognized that her relationship with Carl no longer served her. However, it also dragged on quite a bit longer than it needed to. I don't think that we needed the "days turned into weeks turned into months" epilogue.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: The timeline here felt a little bit unclear. The first half of the story, which covered Emma's early days in college and her road trip with Lizzy, Martin, and Carl, felt fine, but then it jumped forward in spurts to talk about her ongoing academic studies. There was an "as days turned into weeks and months" flash forward, and we ended with Emma as an adult professional reflecting back on her college days. None of that felt necessary or balanced.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The entire story was presented more as summary than scene. The adage is that writers need to "show not tell," and this story was almost completely "telling.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There were no turns in the story. Everything significant that happened, like Emma ending her relationship with Carl, was very clearly forecast in the text.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: We don't get a ton of the other characters in the beginning of the story, but we do get to sit with Carl and hear about his own growth at the end, in a path that's paralleled Emma's. We learn that their break-up served both of them well. So it wasn't just Emma that got good character development.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: There's very little interiority in the manuscript -- we're told what Emma is thinking and feeling, but that's not the same as true interiority, which is (as mentioned above) "showing" us by immersing us into Emma's POV and experiences. We also don't get any pieces of exteriority like dialogue; there's none present in the story.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The story progresses chronologically, and is about a young woman in college learning how to balance her personal relationships with her own growth and studies. None of that is wholly original.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I suppose that a reader could follow Emma's journey and take away the message that it's a good and worthwhile pursuit to focus on yourself and your own interests and personal and professional development, even over other people in your life. But I wouldn't say that's the point of the story, and it's hardly a unique or original idea.

Originality in Thought.explanation: As discussed above, the entire premise of the story -- a young woman in college learning how to balance her relationships and her personal growth and studies -- is hardly original.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The story tries in the beginning. ("The coffee shop was buzzing with energy as the scent of freshly ground beans filled the air.") But that ambition is brief and quickly abandoned.

Character Development.explanation: I wouldn't say that no character feels like they're present simply to fulfill a plot requirement -- Lizzy and Martin drop out pretty quickly, and Johan is only mentioned once, clearly as a remnant from some sort of prompt. But Emma is given significant character development, and Carl, the only other prominent character, is very intentionally given development to match Emma's own.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There is zero subtext in this story. As mentioned earlier, the story is awful at "telling not showing." The entire thing reads like a synopsis of a story rather than a story itself.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: There is no narrative propulsion to this story, nor a beginning, middle, or end. The story only describes various scenes of Stella interacting with Martin, Johan, and Lizzy. There is no plot to speak of -- except of, perhaps, Stella's growing dislike of Martin, although that's a stretch -- and it ends abruptly.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: There is so much overwrought idiom and allusion in this story that it's clear the importance of such was fed into an AI prompt. "Martin was another envelope addressed to the past, and like the many other letters, undeserving of postage." "She could feel the weight of them on her soul, like heavy coins in a rusted tin box." "Their friendship was a slow burn, with the occasional scalding, like hot wax dripping onto Stella's hand and filling in the spaces between her fingers." It's so clunky!

Narrative Ending.explanation: The story ends incredibly abruptly, in media res. There's no real ending, it just... stops right in the middle of a paragraph.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: There's no real sense of time here -- it just describes various scenes, and it's mostly unclear how they relate or are situated with one another. They each exist wholly in their own space.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: This story is only scenes -- there are too many scenes! -- but, yes, there are scenes present, as well as summary, and they feel... reasonably balanced, I guess? It's not well executed, but it's there.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There are no turns! It's impossible to have a turn when there's no plot.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: Yes, the story provides the perspectives of Stella and Martin, as well as Johan and Lizzy. Although they're not all presented convincingly and accurately: Martin seems to be well-liked at first, but then is suddenly disliked with no real explanation as to why the transition took place. It's explained that he's loud, gregarious, and talks too much -- that he can't read the room -- but there's no transition between liking him and not. We like him in one scene, we don't in the next.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: I wouldn't really say there's any interiority here. There are certainly attempts, but they're rather nonsensical. ("Stella liked Johan because he was foreign and probably lonely, and more importantly, elegant. The fact that he was already entrenched in the PhD program was a source of comfort for her—his future was as impenetrable as her past seemed.") Stella liked Johan because he was foreign and probably lonely? How does that make sense?

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: I suppose you could say that the story is original such that there's no plot and simply a collection of mostly unrelated scenes, but I don't think that's an intentionally original decision so much as it is a lack of skill.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: There are zero takeaways here. How could there be? There's no plot or character development!

Originality in Thought.explanation: I... guess there are no clichés? The good news about nonsensical phrasing and no plot is that it's all original! ("Time travel, Stella thought to herself, must be reserved for memories, as only therein can humans experience both pain and pleasure without the physical strain.") It sounds like a cliché, but it's actually so nonsensical that I'm sure nobody's said it before.

World Building and Setting.explanation: There are no sensory details present in the text.

Character Development.explanation: There is no character development present in the text. It's hard to have any development, when the timeline of the story is unclear and it's not really known how the scenes relate to one another.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation:
There's really no subtext here -- everything is spelled out for the reader in painful detail. ("The fifth time Stella saw Martin, she was starting to feel his weight on her scale. "Hey, Stella! he bellowed, stretching out her name like a pair of pants that had narrowly stopped fitting.

She fought back a sigh.")

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story does not follow a conventional narrative arc but it's nevertheless engaging. The series of images presented come together through the narrator's voice and the impact they have on her life.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The author shows a skillful manipulation of language. One remarkable instance is when condoms are compared to 'dry petals, a thumb brace, masking tape.'

Narrative Ending.explanation: As the story does not follow a conventional arc, the ending doesn't provide a definitive answer to the protagonist's problems. The ending connects with the opening of the piece through the reference to a naked woman holding a machine gun, and cleverly morphs that image with the sculpture of the Venus of Willendorf.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: This is a very short piece but it feels packed with action and there is a sense of the character's development through her relationships with the men in her life. The author is skilled at using short sentences to accelerate the time of the story.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: Specific scenes are very vivid, such as when the protagonist is slapped. This is well-balanced with other moments when the relationships between the other characters are summarised.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: This story isn't trying to be surprising, however certain scenes catch the reader off-guard and add to the narration. An example is the slap scene, but generally the story isn't concerned with twists.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The male characters in the story tend to blend together slightly, this is a possible fault of the shortness of the piece and the breezy tone it adopts. However the secondary characters serve to show new and interesting facets of the protagonist.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: This question doesn't necessarily apply to this story. This is because the narrator is intentionally avoiding introspection, it's a story about casual sex and encounters and not thinking much about its consequences. There is a sense that the protagonist is hiding what they would like to say or how they feel, which suggests an interiority which we don't get access to; for that reason I would give the story a pass.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: This kind of story isn't new and pervades in many autofiction narrations. The author, while keeping the reader engaged, doesn't do enough to be qualified as original. An interesting use of images and description is the closest it amounts to originality in form.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: As said in my previous answer, this isn't a new kind of narrative, but a new take on a popular kind of autofiction writing. I would say that the reader obtains a new perspective rather than a unique and original idea.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The story very deftly avoids clichés. A way it does so is by keeping its descriptions short and its images fresh. An example would be the description of the Practical Pig: 'He looks like a member of the Ku Klux Klan. The American South. Mangrove swamps. Banjo on the porch. Root beer. Cornbread. Violence.'

World Building and Setting.explanation: There is little sensory description of the world that these characters inhabit, but what we get is enough to imagine the rest. The first paragraph is one of the most sensory, with its description of black mould on the walls. Another image that stood out to me was: 'I embrace him. He is moist and engorged.'

Character Development.explanation: This is a tricky question to answer since, as this is a flash fiction piece, there isn't enough time nor the need to develop each character fully. There is a sketch of the narrator's feelings and the sort of people she relates with. I wouldn't necessarily fault the story for this lack of development, however. After all it succeeds at what it's trying to do: capture a young person's feelings and experiences at a very particular period in her life.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: By leaving out many things, the story hints at a rich undergrowth of sensations and feelings. The final paragraph is a very skilled use of subtext through the reference to ancient erotic art.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story has such a predictable and uninteresting plot line that it fails to be engaging or satisfying. The repeated reliance on trite images and sentiments bars any sensible reader from engaging with the piece in a meaningful way.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: There are some laughable attempts at metaphor. One of these occurs at the end of the story: 'Jane grasped Johan's hand tightly, navigating into uncharted waters with her compass pointing due north, toward the future - and toward love.' This isn't sophisticated or even insightful.

Narrative Ending.explanation: The ending fails to resolve any of the problems set up by the story in a satisfactory way. Instead we get a fairytale ending that reeks of conformism.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: There is no attempt at compression of time. The story is straightforward and tricks the reader into a straightforward conclusion.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: There are some very bad paragraphs where the narrator discusses her friend's relationships in very dry and uninteresting terms. These do not add to the narrative but instead give the whole text a feeling of unreality.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There are no turns per se, and the problems set up at the beginning are resolved in a predictable way. The narrative arc is very flat and disappointing.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: The perspective of the protagonist feels so detached from any sense of reality that we can't imagine it's convincing or accurate. It feels like a robotic attempt at understanding how humans feel about other people.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: There is no heart or real observation in this story. It has the same emotional range that is so distinguishable in AI-generated stories: a character has a challenge to overcome, certain obstacles come up but they are eventually resolved and the protagonist learns from their experience. Such a trite formula does not lead to 'creative' or valuable writing.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: As I've described in my previous answer, the structure is not original but rather a recycled formula. What was interesting about the 1st story (descriptions of sexual desire, catchy images) are watered down to a parody of itself, which lacks all the formal inventiveness of the previous story.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: The recylcing of forms and shallowness of thought will fail to make an impact on any discerning reader. The story is too transparent about what it's trying to achieve or how it's trying to make the reader feel, which is never a good thing in literature.

Originality in Thought.explanation: The form is full of clichés and so is the writing. This becomes especially apparent in the romantic descriptions: 'Being with Johan felt reckless and alive.' These fail to convey any emotion to the reader.

World Building and Setting.explanation: There are no attempts at realistic world building precisely because the story is rooted in cliché and outdated forms. Besides there are no descriptions of the world that these people inhabit.

Character Development.explanation: The sensations that the protagonist experiences do not feel real or relatable. Instead they seem like the product of a bad TV script, or an unsuccessful attempt at a sitcom.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: The text operates on a single, surface level throughout. The attempt at tying together the protagonist's assessment of her friend's relationship problems and her own successful relationship is not effective.

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: The story is too long and loses the reader's attention throughout. Just like the previous story, it is too transparent about its intetions, which it fails to accomplish.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The images are overused and bland. There is a lack of specificity which makes the whole reading experience vague and uninteresting. An example of such image is this: the 'scent of freshly ground beans' — not terrible, but not good either.

Narrative Ending.explanation: There are several turns where we are led to believe the story is about to end, but then it does not. So when the ending finally comes it's disappointing.

Narrative Pacing.explanation: There is a very clumsy attempt at time compression in this text. This is signalled by the opening of the paragraph usually: 'Days turned into weeks, and weeks turned into months [...] As days turned into weeks and months.' This is not sufficient to keep us interested or to keep an accurate track of the timeline of the story.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: There is little distinction between scene and summary. The scenes feel like they're being glazed over, almost like summaries themselves.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There are too many turns to keep track of. None of these are interesting, and their abundance makes them tiresome.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: We only really get the protagonist's perspective, and it does not feel convincing or compleling. This is in part due to the excess of clichés.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: There isn't a successful description of the characters' interiority. We are only offered reductive explanations for their actions.

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: The structure of the story doesn't hold together. It's too long and unfocused, the opposite of what makes a flash fiction piece work.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: The average reader will be bored by this story and put it down. There is no substance to it, no reason to keep reading it. It isn't informed by a discerning, authoritative mind who is organising thoughts in a beautiful or original arrangement.

Originality in Thought.explanation: What passes as psychological insight in this story is simply clichéd self-help talk. This is an example: 'She was excited to take on the next chapter, eager to see where her journey would lead her.'

World Building and Setting.explanation: The clichéd ideas and images fail to make the world of the story believable. 'And as the coffee shop continued to buzz with the trappings of student life...'. This does not capture what being in a coffee shop actually feels like.

Character Development.explanation: The protagonist goes through several transformations and events, but there is no sense of real development. This is because the ending is too clearly manufactured to deliver a message.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: There is no subtext. Instead we are offered the language of business and corporations: 'single-minded focus,' 'reconnecting on a deeper level,' 'the power of personal growth and following one's personal path.'

Understandability and Coherence.explanation: There is hardly a narrative. The story feels loose and unfinished.

Language Proficiency and Literary Device.explanation: The writer overindulges in bad clichés and excessive metaphors. One example (of many): ' Painful memories were a reminder to Stella that she had grown and evolved, the college campus serving as her growth rings.' This borders on parody, but it lacks the self-awareness to be called that.

Narrative Ending.explanation: There is no resolution to the very basic plot elements raised by the story. The story simply drops off at the end

Narrative Pacing.explanation: There are some attempts at manipulating time, but these don't lead anywhere. The story is clumsily divided in different sections which don't contribute to the development of the plot.

Scenes vs. Summaries.explanation: The scenes are unsatisfactory despite some poor attempts at dialogue and description. This is mostly because of the exasperating metaphors and strained similes the author indulges in.

Structural Flexibility.explanation: There aren't any turns. The protagonist falls for a man, then for another one, and picks him in the end.

Perspective and Voice Flexibility.explanation: We only get one perspective which is hardly developed or satisfactory. There is an attempt to introduce other perspectives through dialogue, but this is so mediocre that it fails to accomplish that.

Emotional Flexibility.explanation: There is no interiority as seen in the ending which does not fit into the rest of the story or is justified in any way by the protagonist's earlier motivations. There is a fan fiction-y tone to the piece and to its (lack of) emotional development

Originality in Form and Structure.explanation: There is no originality of form here. The story is poorly structured and fails to resolve even the most basic of plot elements.

Originality in Theme and Content.explanation: I can't imagine the reader would get anything from this story other than a recycled perception of romance. The story is also unfinished, which doesn't do it any favours.

Originality in Thought.explanation: There is an exasperating amount of cliché. This line is an example: 'The hunger she had felt earlier was somewhat satiated, but she knew it would never be entirely extinguished.' It is neither illuminating or original.

World Building and Setting.explanation: The author mostly relies on vague and unconvincing metaphors, which do not capture the likeness of real life. An example is this sentence: 'Stella found herself reminiscing about the tightrope she had been traveling on during her first year at university, where the landscape bordered the unmanageable and ungovernable.' It fails to create an accurate image of the university.

Character Development.explanation: The character of Stella feels flat and shallow. This is because her actions at the end of the story are dissonant from the earlier parts of the story.

Rhetorical Complexity.explanation: The story fails to even tell a convincing tale, let alone have any implication of subtext. While the previous two stories were very clumsy at delivering a message, at least they had a message to offer.
